faq.a: The lateral malleolus forms the lateral wall of the ankle mortise; its loss allows talar shift and lateral ligament rupture.
faq.q: Why does a distal fibular fracture destabilise the ankle?

faq.a: It raises suspicion for associated tibial fracture, pelvic injury, or vascular damage, requiring full trauma assessment.
faq.q: What is the significance of a high‑energy mechanism in a fibular shaft fracture?

faq.a: Yes, most isolated shaft fractures are treated with functional bracing or casting if alignment is acceptable.
faq.q: Can a fibular fracture heal without surgery?

exam: A 25‑year‑old motorcyclist presents with lateral ankle swelling after a fall – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform an AP and lateral ankle X‑ray to identify fracture pattern and assess ankle stability.

A patient with a proximal fibular fracture develops foot drop – what nerve is injured and what does this indicate? — The peroneal nerve is injured; it signals need for urgent neuro‑vascular assessment and possible surgical decompression.

You suspect compartment syndrome in a leg with a fibular shaft fracture but lack a pressure monitor – how do you proceed? — Rely on clinical signs (pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense swelling) and perform emergent fasciotomy if confirmed.

Explain why a Weber C distal fibular fracture often requires surgical fixation. — The fracture is above the syndesmosis, disrupting ankle stability; surgery restores the mortise and prevents chronic instability.

In a low‑resource setting, how would you manage an open fibular fracture with limited antibiotics? — Clean wound thoroughly, give a broad‑spectrum injectable antibiotic (e.g., ceftriaxone) if available, and arrange timely debridement and fixation.

What examination finding differentiates a simple fibular fracture from an associated ankle ligament injury? — Positive talar tilt or anterior drawer test indicates ligament disruption beyond the bone injury.

A child presents with a greenstick fibular fracture – what is the appropriate immobilisation? — Apply a long leg cast or splint with the knee flexed 30° to maintain alignment while allowing some motion.
Why is the fibula a preferred donor site for bone grafts in tibial non‑union? — It provides cortical bone without compromising weight‑bearing, and harvesting has low morbidity.
ai.title: Fibula Anatomy and Clinical Significance
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The fibula is the slender lateral bone of the lower leg that provides attachment for muscles and stabilises the ankle. Understanding its anatomy helps diagnose fractures, ankle instability and compartment syndrome, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Proximal end: head, neck, and lateral tibial plateau articulation
Distal end: lateral malleolus articulates with talus and calcaneus
sections.p: The fibula runs parallel to the tibia from the knee joint to the lateral malleolus. It does not bear weight but forms the lateral ankle mortise and serves as a lever for several leg muscles.

b: Peroneal (fibular) nerve runs just posterior to the fibular neck – vulnerable in proximal fractures
Distal fibular fracture (Weber type) predicts lateral ankle ligament injury
Fibular shaft fracture can be a marker for high‑energy trauma
sections.p: Clinically the fibula matters for ankle stability, peroneal nerve protection, and as a source of donor bone for grafts. Its fractures often accompany tibial injury and can mask compartment syndrome.

b: Assess for distal fibular fracture when patient has lateral ankle swelling or inability to evert foot
Check for peroneal nerve palsy – foot drop, loss of sensation over dorsum of foot
Monitor for signs of compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense swelling
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, fibular fractures are common after road‑traffic accidents and falls. Prompt recognition prevents malunion, chronic ankle instability and compartment syndrome, which can lead to limb loss.

t.b: Confirms fracture location and pattern; guides casting vs surgery
Answers whether pressure >30 mm Hg; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs
